### What the default OpenMapTiles / OSM‑based vector style expects

The shield‑rendering layers that come with the **OpenMapTiles** (or any of the “OSM‑Bright / OSM‑Liberty”‑style basemaps) use a **single `icon-image` expression** that builds the sprite name from the feature’s `network` and `ref_length` properties:
Because of that, the style looks for **exactly** the following sprite IDs (the part after the final “/” in the sprite URL, i.e. the key in the `sprite.json` file).

column1: > `ref_length` is the number of characters in the `ref` string (e.g. `I‑5` → length 2, `US‑101` → length 3). The style uses that length to pick a badge that is sized appropriately for the number of digits.

If the sprite you are pointing at **does not contain one of those IDs**, the badge simply does not draw – you see only the numeric text (which comes from the `text-field` expression, not from the sprite).

Below is a **step‑by‑step recipe** that turns “green‑and‑brown icons disappear on a photo” into “icons are readable on any satellite / aerial tile”.
All the techniques are taken from the **MapLibre‑Cartography** skill, so they work with the current MapLibre GL JS API (v2.x‑v3.x).

column3: Why it happens
The park is also green → the icon’s chroma (saturation) is the same as the background, so the eye can’t separate them.
The soil already has a brown‑ish hue → the same problem.
The background can be bright, dark, saturated or desaturated at any pixel under the icon. A plain‑color sprite has no “edge” that the eye can latch onto.

column1: The only things you can **control** in a WebGL canvas are the **icon’s own color, its edge treatment (halo / outline / shadow), and its shape**.
## 2. Choose the right *base* colour for the icon

column3: Recommended colour family

Use a **high‑saturation earth tone that is *outside* the typical vegetation / soil palette** – e.g. **amber / terracotta / burnt‑orange** (`#e65100`), **deep teal** (`#006d6d`), or **vivid magenta** (`#c6007e`).

column2: **Keep the semantic meaning** (if you need “green = park”)
column3: Keep the *fill* a **tint** of the semantic colour (e.g. `#c8f5cc` for parks) **and rely on the halo/outline for contrast** (see below).

column1: > **Rule of thumb:** *If the colour you are already using can be found in a typical aerial image, pick a different hue.* The hue itself is less important than the **contrast of the edge**.
## 3. Give every icon an **SDF halo** (the most flexible solution)
* **SDF = Signed Distance Field** – a greyscale image where the alpha is derived from the distance to the shape edge.
* MapLibre can draw a **stroke/halo** around the shape *without* you having to bake it into the PNG.

column2: **Convert your SVG to an SDF PNG** (recommended tools)
column3:
`spritezero --sdf ./src-icons ./out-sprite`
or
`spreet --sdf ./icons ./sprite`

**Host the sprite** on the same origin (or a CDN with CORS) and set the style’s `sprite` property to the base URL (no extension).

> If you only have a handful of icons, you can also load them at runtime:
// Example for a single custom SVG
""icon-halo-color"": ""rgba(0,0,0,0.75)"",   // dark semi‑transparent works on any bright/dark background
""icon-halo-width"": 1.2,                  // 1–2 px is enough; increase for very small icons
// optional: a subtle inner glow for extra contrast
* The **dark, semi‑transparent halo** (`rgba(0,0,0,0.75)`) creates a *figure‑ground* edge that is visible on bright fields (soil, rooftops) **and on dark fields (forest canopy, water)**.
* Because the halo is drawn **outside the icon’s vector shape**, it does **not** increase the icon’s visual weight like a thick outline would.
* The **high‑saturation fill** (`#e65100`) stays distinguishable even when the halo is thin.
## 4. If you cannot use SDF (raster PNG icons)
Sometimes you have a raster PNG (e.g. a photo of a sign) that you cannot rebuild as SDF. In that case you have two options:
### 4.1. Bake a halo into the PNG itself
* Add a **stroke** (2–3 px) around the shape in a dark colour.
* Add a **soft outer glow** (Gaussian blur, ~4 px) in the same dark colour.
* Export the PNG with a **transparent margin** (extra canvas space) so the halo isn’t clipped.
> This is a *static* solution – you lose the ability to change the halo colour or width at runtime.
### 4.2. Add a **separate “background” circle layer** under the icon
""circle-radius"": [""+"", [""zoom""], 2],   // a bit larger than the icon
*The circle is drawn **first**, so the icon sits on top of a dark, slightly larger disc that works as a halo.*
*If you need a different shape (square, star) you can use a `fill-extrusion` or a custom SDF sprite instead.*
## 5. Add a **contact‑shadow** for a 3‑D feel (optional but powerful)
A simple drop‑shadow makes the icon appear to **lie on the ground** instead of floating, which further separates it from the photo.
""icon-shadow-offset"": [0, 2]   // 2 px down, matches hillshade illumination (NW → shadows point SE)
*The shadow colour should be a **dark, semi‑transparent** value; the blur should be soft (1–2 px).
*If you use a raster PNG you must bake the shadow into the image or use the separate‑circle‑layer trick described above.*
At very low zooms the icon may be only a few pixels wide; a **relative halo width** keeps the edge visible.

The halo works the same because it is dark‑transparent.

Also mention layer ordering, figure-ground, accessibility. Provide steps.
**No – lowering the opacity of the OSM Bright road layers is the wrong fix.**

A semi‑transparent orange/yellow road on top of a photographic basemap will let the busy texture of the imagery bleed through, making the road look “washed‑out” and still visually noisy. The proper solution is to **re‑tone the road palette for imagery** and keep the roads **opaque**, using width, value (light‑dark), and subtle contrast instead of hue and transparency.
Below is a step‑by‑step guide that follows the cartographic principles in the **maplibre‑cartography** skill.
## 1. Why opacity hurts more than it helps

column3: What happens when you set `road-opacity < 1`
The underlying satellite texture (trees, roofs, fields) shows through the road fill, adding visual “noise” that competes with the road line itself.
The orange/yellow hue is already high‑saturation; making it translucent only mixes it with whatever the imagery pixel is, producing a muddy, unpredictable colour.
Opacity reduces the perceived “weight” of the road, making it harder to read at low zoom where only a few major roads are shown.
Contrast calculations (WCAG) are done against the *combined* colour (road + imagery). A semi‑transparent road can fall below the 4.5:1 ratio for many background pixels.

column1: The cartographic rule of thumb for overlaying vector data on imagery is **“keep the overlay opaque and tone it down, not transparent.”**
## 2. Re‑tone the road palette for imagery
Replace the bright orange/yellow palette with a **neutral‑grey hierarchy**. The visual hierarchy is then expressed by **width** and **value contrast** (light vs. dark), not by hue.
// Example for a generic “road” layer (OSM Bright style)
10, ""#5a5a5a"",   // dark grey at low zoom (when only a thin line shows)
18, ""#a0a0a0""    // light grey at high zoom (when many roads appear)
The casing should be **darker than the fill** and also opaque. This gives the road a crisp edge without a harsh black “cartoon” outline.
// Casing is a little wider than the fill
* **Neutral greys** do not compete with the many colours in imagery.
* **Opaque fills** give a solid visual anchor; the road stays readable even over bright fields or dark forests.
* **Width hierarchy** (thin at low zoom, thick at high zoom) still tells the user which roads are more important.
* **Value contrast** (lighter fill, darker casing) provides the same “pop” that hue used to give, but without clashing with the background.
### 2.3 Optional: subtle hue for semantic meaning
If you need a hint of semantics (e.g., motorways a faint blue, rail a muted brown), keep the hue **very low‑saturation** (≤ 15 %). Example:

If you truly need a visual “fade‑out” at very low zoom (e.g., to avoid a dense web of tiny roads), do it **by zoom‑based width** and **by turning the layer off** at those zooms, not by lowering opacity.
## 4. Layer ordering – make sure roads sit **under** labels but **above** the imagery
